stakeholders.said: "We're writing more business than ever and making less money on it. Where is the money going?"
stakeholders.answer: Three leaks: broker B07 (~$428,950 excess), Montréal Home water (~$360,684), and Home pricing that ignores risk. B07 alone explains the 2026 deterioration (loss ratio 0.9 → 0.58 without it).

stakeholders.said: "My teams are drowning. Some offices are fine, others aren't. I need more adjusters."

stakeholders.answer: Customers whose claim took more than 30 days did not renew 55% vs about 16–17% when it closed sooner (more than 20 days: 36% vs 16%). The effect is not about price.

stakeholders.said: "Brokers are our best growth engine. Don't slow them down."
stakeholders.answer: The channel is healthy without B07 (Auto through brokers is as profitable as through agents). Do not slow brokers in general; do put one broker on hold, and add automatic monitors for all.

issues.title: Broker B07 writes business that claims immediately and just under the review threshold
issues.oneLiner: 60 theft claims where about 2.6 were expected; loss ratio 4.29; 83% of its claims sit just under $10,000.
issues.conclusion: B07 explains the entire 2026 deterioration ("more business, less money"). The pattern (early theft claims, amounts just below senior review, no denials) is consistent with organised early-claim fraud or severe adverse selection. It needs investigation, not a verdict.

why.test: Is it Toronto-wide theft rather than one broker?
why.result: Toronto theft outside B07 is 0.026 per policy-year, the same as the book (0.032); B07 runs 0.72

why.test: Is it the timing of claims?

why.test: Are claim amounts shaped around the review line?

why.test: Are claims scrutinised normally?
why.result: 0 of 70 B07 claims were denied versus 5.3% elsewhere (chance of zero denials ≈ 2.2%), and 77% went to Team A

why.test: Is every broker like this?
why.result: No other broker exceeds 30% early-claim share or 13% near-threshold share

why.test: Is it a data error?
why.result: All 173 B07 policies start in 2026 and pass the same cleaning as the rest; the pattern survives removing duplicates and re-parsing dates

why.test: Is it fraud or adverse selection?
why.result: The data cannot separate organised fraud from a poorly screened book; both call for the same first action (hold and review)

decision.what: Place B07 on hold (stop new binding and renewals), freeze payment of unpaid B07 claims pending review, and open an SIU file on its policies and its 70 claims.
decision.where: Broker B07 (173 policies; Toronto 104, Ottawa 29, Montréal 19, other 21)
decision.when: Hold today; SIU triage of the near-threshold claims within 30 days; review commission clawback under the broker contract
decision.how: Distribution suspends binding authority; Claims routes any B07 claim to senior review regardless of amount; SIU samples applications for ghost-brokering, identity and address mismatches; add the same early-claim and near-threshold monitors for every broker (see automation R1 and R2).
decision.why: The book excluding B07 runs a 0.62 loss ratio; with B07 it is 0.702. Fixing one broker recovers about $428,950 of observed excess cost without slowing the other nine brokers.
decision.expected: Book loss ratio 0.702 → 0.62; about $428,950 of observed excess cost stops accruing
decision.confidence: High that the pattern is abnormal (probability under chance < 1e-12); medium on the cause
decision.ifWrong: The hold is reversible: if SIU clears the claims, release payments, reinstate the broker and keep the monitors

issues.oneLiner: Home water claims are 3× Toronto's per policy-year and the price does not reflect it (Montréal avg $1,235 vs Toronto $1,416).

why.test: Is it one sales channel?
why.result: Ratio by channel: Agent ×3.2, Broker ×2.7, Online ×3.1

why.test: Is it the deductible mix?

why.result: Cohort ratios 2025H1 ×4.5, 2025H2 ×1.8, 2026H1 ×2.9; the most water claims on any single Montréal day is 2

why.test: Is it "Quebec" (province rules, Team C coding)?

decision.what: Add a Montréal water-territory factor to Home rating. Step 1: +36% (moves our Montréal/Toronto price relativity from 0.87 to the market's 1.19; PolicyMe 2026 quotes: Montréal $2,868 vs Toronto $2,412, one house profile). Step 2: require or credit a backwater valve and shut-off device, and raise the water deductible. Hold new Montréal Home business from brokers until the factor is live.
decision.where: Home · Montréal island (no postal data yet; refine by postal area once collected)
decision.when: File before the next renewal cycle; run the valve/inspection outreach in February, before the March–May peak; re-measure after spring 2027
decision.how: Actuarial: re-fit water frequency with a Montréal factor (indicated break-even premium $3,058 vs $1,235 today, 148%), phase to market parity first because customers can shop (Ratehub: 57% switched after a price rise). Underwriting: add backwater valve, sump pump and building-age questions at quote.
decision.why: At today's price a Montréal Home policy loses about $1,276 a year after expenses; the parity step moves the combined ratio from 2.03 to 1.57 but does not fully close it, which is why mitigation and exposure control must come with it.

decision.confidence: High that the problem is real and unpriced; medium on the size of the right rate (no property data, regulatory filing needed)
risks: Regulatory review of a territory factor
Peer-city events (Toronto 2024, Ottawa 2026) show water is not unique to Montréal
decision.ifWrong: If the Montréal gap shrinks after property data is added, keep the factor only for the segments where the excess persists

issues.oneLiner: Home loss ratio 1.03 vs Auto 0.53; Home Medium band 1.29 vs High 0.98.

why.test: Is Home really the money-loser?

why.test: Does Auto price follow risk while Home does not?

why.result: High premium is 42% above Medium for 19% more claims

why.test: Does city enter the Home price?
why.result: Average Home premium ranges only $1,114–$1,416 while cost per policy-year ranges $537–$2,140

why.test: Is the $500 deductible under-priced?

why.test: Could this be a catastrophe year or noise?

decision.what: Re-rate Home: add a water territory factor (Montréal first), rebalance Medium and High bands using frequency and severity, and tighten the $500 deductible credit. Do not raise Auto prices.

decision.when: Next rate filing; validate the bands on 2026 claims before filing
decision.how: Re-fit frequency and severity with city, band and deductible, check lift by band, and apply credibility (13 fire claims earn about 11% weight; Medium/High have hundreds). The indicated changes above are screening numbers, not a filing.

issues.title: Waiting for a claim to close drives non-renewal
issues.oneLiner: Customers whose claim took more than 30 days did not renew 55% of the time versus 17% (n=84 vs 368); at 20 days it is 36% vs 16%.
issues.conclusion: The Head of Retention is right. Waits up to 30 days barely move renewal, but beyond 30 days non-renewal jumps to more than three times the baseline; the effect survives restricting to small claims and is not about price. So the hard line is 30 days, with 20 days as the working target.

why.test: Does the effect rise steadily with the wait?
Is it just big claims being slow and unhappy?
why.result: Among claims under $10,000 only, waits over 20 days did not renew 32% (n=130) vs 17% (n=273)

why.test: Is it the claim outcome (denial) rather than the wait?
why.result: Customers with a denied claim: 26% non-renewal vs 24% otherwise (n=31)

why.test: Is it price?
why.result: Non-renewal by premium quartile: 17% / 16% / 16% / 17% (flat)

why.test: Is the cut-off cherry-picked?
why.result: Best cut-off found by search was 30 days (55% vs 17%); at the plain 20-day line it is 36% vs 16%. The buckets show a cliff after 30 days rather than a smooth slope, so the 30-day line is the one to defend

decision.what: Set a 30-day hard limit and a 20-day working target; send proactive status updates at day 7 and day 14, and make a retention call for any claim still open at day 14 so none crosses day 30.
decision.where: All claims; start with Team C where 38 of 48 open claims sit
decision.when: Alerts live now (automation R3); measure renewals on the next two cohorts
decision.how: Daily job lists open claims older than 14 days, ranks them by premium at risk, and creates tasks for the adjuster and a retention call (see R3).
decision.why: Each excess non-renewal costs about $1,557 of premium; in this sample the slow-claim gap is about $49,952.
decision.expected: Non-renewal after slow claims falls toward the 16% baseline
decision.confidence: Medium: observational; satisfaction research supports speed and communication (J.D. Power 2025) but is mostly US and stated intent
risks: Proactive calls on denied claims can backfire
Slow claims may also be harder claims
decision.ifWrong: If renewal does not improve after speed improves, redirect effort to claim outcome and price

issues.oneLiner: Claims ≥ $10,000 take 30 days (vs 13); Team C intake is 2.07× its earlier pace and holds 38 of 48 open claims.
issues.conclusion: The VP of Claims is partly right: Team C is overloaded, but adding adjusters alone will not fix the largest delays, which come from the approval step on large Water Damage claims. Process and authority design is the faster lever, with temporary capacity for Team C during the March–May and October peaks.

why.test: Are large claims slower because of the $10,000 review?

why.test: Is it only Team C being slow?

why.test: What fills the senior-review queue?
why.result: 41 of the 88 large claims (47%) are Water Damage, the Montréal peril; Team C reviews 42 of 88

why.test: Does the threshold distort behaviour?
why.result: Claims at $9–10k: 54 (25 without the flagged broker) vs $10–11k: 15 (15); a small bunching remains after removing B07

why.test: Does waiting cost renewals?

decision.what: Create a fast-track lane for Water Damage claims between $10,000 and about $25,000 (documented, photo and contractor estimate, not from a flagged source) with team-lead approval inside 5 business days; keep full senior review above that. Add temporary adjuster capacity to Team C for March–May and October. Set a 20-day claim target with automatic ageing alerts.
decision.where: Claims: Team C (Montréal + Québec City) first; fast-track rule for all teams
decision.when: Staff Team C before March; pilot the fast-track for one quarter; ageing alerts start now (automation R3)
decision.how: Raise delegated authority for a defined claim class only, with a 10% random audit and an automatic escalation for claims within 20% under the new line (the B07 detector). Use the claims-in-progress figure (≈ intake × cycle days ÷ 30) to size capacity: 15.4 now vs 7.4 before.
decision.why: Slow claims cost renewals: moving half of the 165 slow claims under 20 days protects roughly $25,679 of annual premium in this sample, and it addresses the Retention complaint at its source.
decision.expected: Median large-claim close from 30 toward 20 days; non-renewal after slow claims falls toward the 16% baseline
decision.confidence: Medium: the delay-to-churn link is observational, and the fast-track must not reopen the fraud route the B07 pattern exploits

decision.ifWrong: If cycle time does not fall in the pilot quarter, revert authority and add capacity instead

issues.title: Bundled customers are better risks: a growth lever with a caveat
issues.oneLiner: Bundled customers: 0.214 claims per policy-year vs 0.277; loss ratio 0.66 vs 0.75.
issues.conclusion: Bundled customers claim less and cost less, but they do not renew more in this data, so the benefit is lower loss cost, not retention. Test a bundle offer with a holdout group to separate selection from effect.

why.test: Do bundled customers cost less?
why.result: Claims per policy-year 0.214 vs 0.277; loss ratio 0.66 vs 0.75

why.test: Do they stay longer?
why.result: Non-renewal 16.5% vs 16.6%: no retention difference in this data (J.D. Power US reports 95% vs 85%, a different population)

why.test: Is it the bundle or the customer?
why.result: Better customers choose bundles (selection), so the discount should be tested, not assumed

decision.what: Run a bundle offer test on single-line Auto customers with a holdout group.
decision.where: Single-line customers in Calgary, Toronto, Ottawa (not Montréal Home until water is priced)
decision.how: Randomise the offer; measure claims, retention and margin after 12 months.
decision.why: Bundled customers claim less and renew more in this book.
decision.expected: Lower loss cost per policy if the effect is causal; no retention gain assumed
decision.ifWrong: End the test if the holdout shows no difference

automations.name: Broker hold on early-claim + threshold pattern
automations.condition: Broker with ≥ 15 claims where early-claim (≤ 45 days) share or near-threshold ($8–10k) share is improbable versus the book (binomial tail < 1e-6)

actions.do: Suspend new binding and renewals for the broker
Open SIU file on policies and claims
Route every claim from this broker to senior review regardless of amount

automations.ifWrong: A hold is a review, not a termination; if SIU clears the broker, payments are released and the broker reinstated. False alarms cost a few weeks of binding.

automations.name: Near-threshold claim audit
automations.condition: Any claim between 80% and 100% of the $10,000 senior-review line, or any group whose share in that band exceeds 3× the book

actions.do: Send all flagged-broker near-threshold claims to senior review
Sample 25% of other near-threshold claims for audit

automations.ifWrong: Wasted review time on honest claims; mitigated by sampling only 25% outside flagged sources.

automations.name: Ageing-claim escalation and retention call
automations.condition: Open or under-review claim older than 14 days (the 20-day line minus a 6-day buffer)

actions.do: Move to the priority queue and ask the adjuster for a status update
Escalate claims ≥ $10,000 to the fast-track reviewer

automations.ifWrong: An unnecessary call to a customer whose claim was already moving; low cost.

automations.name: Pricing review ticket
automations.condition: City × product with ≥ 150 policies, combined ratio (loss ratio × (1 + LAE) + expenses) above 1.05, and claim-frequency ratio with 95% CI lower bound above 1.3

actions.do: Open pricing review with the indicated change table
Freeze broker new business in the segment until rated

automations.ifWrong: A review ticket costs analyst time only; no price changes without an actuarial filing.
